Motion capture games · 10 November 2026 · Development diagnostics

RTMPose by default.
A preview at the display’s pace.

Measured: 60.00 display draws/s over 30 seconds at Retina scale, with no frame intervals over 25 ms. Camera/source and pose rates remain separate. This is a display-rendering result, not a 60 FPS camera or inference claim.

The user selected RTMPose after a live comparison and asked for a smooth 60+ preview, explicitly accepting separate camera and pose rates. The old exact-pair viewer only drew when inference-aligned packets arrived. This change preserves one acquisition owner and observation semantics while separating capture, pose delivery and rendering.

Issue #10 · PR #21 · Owning ADR 0006 · Synthetic result JSON

What changed and why

  • RTMDet-nano + RTMPose-m is the development default. MediaPipe remains a comparison option. No person-capacity reduction, skipped detection cadence or altered model precision is used to inflate FPS.
  • Independent current-image and pose streams. One extra bounded preview encoder reads the existing capture owner. Slow inference cannot block camera preview publication; the browser decodes images only on the image channel. The legacy exact-pair endpoint remains available.
  • Display-clock drawing. requestAnimationFrame draws the latest image; telemetry and person-list DOM updates run at 4 Hz. Same-style bones and joints are batched into three stroke passes per body. The opaque canvas requests the browser’s optional low-latency hint.
  • Lower processing overhead. Canonical JSON Schema is compiled once, padded detector-output filtering is vectorized, normalization arrays and ONNX input names are reused. CPU thread bounds and the model-independent anatomical contract remain intact.

The reference uses main’s packet-driven tracking console against the integrated service. Both foreground runs use the same three generated bodies, 30-second measurement, five-second warmup and 2× pixel density. This isolates the viewer’s draw scheduling from inference cadence; synthetic input bypasses pose inference. Earlier measurements under a competing graphics workload were uneven even on an idle page and are not used to claim the clean result. That workload was left untouched and the user paused/closed it before the controlled checks.

Rig: Apple M5 (10 GPU cores), macOS 26.6.2, Chrome 157.0.8103.40, built-in Liquid Retina 2560 × 1664 display. Foreground desktop viewport: 1440 × 1050 CSS pixels; final scale: 2×; warmup: 5 s. No forced frame-rate or VSync-disabling flags were used. All 14 complete two-second windows stayed near the display’s 60 Hz limit. Rendering above that physical refresh limit needs a faster display.

Each runtime stage has five warmup calls and 200 measured calls. Schema rows use the same synthetic three-person observation in the same run. Model rows use constant gray tensors: one detector tensor and one fixed pose crop. They measure execution cost, not detection accuracy, multiplayer capacity or full-pipeline latency. Stage percentiles are not added to claim an end-to-end percentile.

Timing and safety tradeoffs

An independent image can be newer than the latest pose. The display holds an observed skeleton only for matching epoch/source/geometry with a source-time lag of 0–150 ms, then hides it and shows the gap. Newer-than-image poses are also hidden. The hold is presentation only; no positions, identity continuity or scoring decisions are manufactured. Camera and pose messages retain their actual source timestamps. Capture timing remains host read completion, not verified exposure.

Preview and observation publication remain one-slot stores; each pull stream has at most one pending reply. Stop, hidden tabs, source resets and model/camera failures invalidate old images and poses and release task-owned capture resources. The backend’s 500 ms age guard remains, with local pose silence and image silence guards of 500 ms and 1.5 s respectively. These are provisional diagnostic limits, not accepted game collision tolerances.

Integration with current main

The final version preserves the compact tracking console, explicit camera discovery/identification, detailed stage telemetry, stable operator rows, shared high-resolution host clock, drift-free synthetic pacing, tracking stability fixes, experimental Mole Motion and Dodgeball. RTMPose is also both games’ camera default; game input keeps its exact-pair transport and existing scoring/session safety rules. Capture FPS now uses a bounded aggregate capture-count/time window, avoiding inflated rates from short driver bursts.

Actual verification

  • Frozen pnpm installation, canonical binding drift checks, TypeScript/Python type checks, ESLint/Ruff and formatting passed.
  • 342 Vitest tests and 103 pytest tests passed. New cases cover camera preview progress during blocked inference, independent streams sharing capture ownership, stale/incompatible overlays, source epochs, pending decode replacement, delayed old-epoch handshakes, bounded drawing work and resource cleanup.
  • The production frontend build and Git whitespace checks passed.
  • Actual local-server Chrome screenshots were inspected at 1440 × 1050 and 390 × 844, English only. No page-width overflow, page exceptions or console warnings/errors appeared in the final browser run.

Before and after

Every image below uses generated bodies. No participant footage or credentials are embedded. The final screenshots were recaptured at scroll position zero to avoid full-page capture artifacts from offscreen fixed elements.

Reproduce

With the local viewer running, keep its benchmark window visible and foreground. Benchmarks are opt-in and run serially; no browser is downloaded automatically.

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm check
pnpm build
pnpm benchmark:runtime --samples 200 --models
pnpm benchmark:preview --label local-check --duration 30000 --warmup 5000 --scale-factor 2

Use --chrome-executable or CHROME_PATH when installed Chrome is elsewhere; use --scale-factor 1 for a lower-density comparison. Logs, metrics and generated screenshots go to ignored reports/local/. Windows/native target browsers need their own measurements.

Remaining limits

The final performance dataset is synthetic. Physical camera modes, real three-person crossings, recognition accuracy, Windows execution, fast-motion overlay error and externally measured motion-to-display latency remain open M1 gates. Camera and pose rates can be lower than display rate; the synthetic screenshot’s roughly 20 source/pose updates per second is deliberately shown alongside 60 render FPS. A foreground 60 Hz display is the practical ceiling here, and competing GPU workloads or browser power/background policies can reduce it.
